1.pericope_label: And now, O ye priests, this commandment is for you. If ye will not hear, and if ye will not lay it to heart, to give glory unto my name, saith the Lord of hosts, I will even send a curse upon you, and I will curse your blessings: yea, I have cursed them already, because ye do not lay it to heart
debates: Why the priests are charged when the people also sinned
Whether the cursed blessings are the priests dues or the blessings they pronounce
Whether the new decree replaces the covenant with Levi
outliers: Ellicott takes the threat itself to become the covenant in place of the old one
Keil and Delitzsch argues from the tense that the curse has already fallen
Clarke reports a rendering that takes away the shoulder instead of the seed
themes: Silence that works as consent
A blessing turned into its opposite
Sacrificial refuse carried outside the camp
A word known to be sent by what it does

5.pericope_label: My covenant was with him of life and peace; and I gave them to him for the fear wherewith he feared me, and was afraid before my name. The law of truth was in his mouth, and iniquity was not found in his lips: he walked with me in peace and equity, and did turn many away from iniquity. For the priest’s lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of the Lord of hosts
debates: Whether the covenant is with Levi, with the Levites, or with Christ
Whether the fear is the reason for the gift or Levi’s side of the bargain
Whether the priest keeps knowledge by storing it or by speaking it
outliers: Gill answers the temporal reading by the recorded ages of Aaron and Phinehas
Ellicott divides the verse so that each party performs his own part of the covenant
Ellicott quotes a writer on the priests of whom the world knows nothing
themes: A covenant that guarantees life and peace
A law of truth carried in the mouth
Peace with God, with neighbour and with conscience
Three words at the close of a testament

8.pericope_label: But ye are departed out of the way; ye have caused many to stumble at the law; ye have corrupted the covenant of Levi, saith the Lord of hosts. Therefore have I also made you contemptible and base before all the people, according as ye have not kept my ways, but have been partial in the law
debates: Whether the people stumble at the law or in it
Whether the contempt fell once or falls repeatedly
What being partial in the law means
outliers: Ellicott reads the contempt as exactly reversing the promised life and peace
Ellicott notes the priests authority was established by the law they abused
Wesley turns the charge on the contempt of the clergy in his own day
themes: A lamp for the path turned into a stone in it
Teachers who leave the road they point to
A people become a proverb where they go
Justice bent to please great men

10.pericope_label: Have we not all one father? hath not one God created us? why do we deal treacherously every man against his brother, by profaning the covenant of our fathers? Judah hath dealt treacherously, and an abomination is committed in Israel and in Jerusalem; for Judah hath profaned the holiness of the Lord which he loved, and hath married the daughter of a strange god
debates: Who the one father of the opening question is
Whether the treachery is extortion or marriage
Whether the pair cut off are teacher and pupil or watchman and answerer
outliers: Ellicott rejects the Talmudic rendering as unsuitable and philologically precarious
Ellicott supports his rendering from an Arabic phrase in the life of Tamerlane
Clarke holds the divorces were multiplied to make room for the forbidden marriages
themes: Brothers who share one father dealing falsely
A conscience with its bonds already broken
A city with no crier and no answerer left
Neither root nor branch remaining

13.pericope_label: And this have ye done again, covering the altar of the Lord with tears, with weeping, and with crying out, insomuch that he regardeth not the offering any more. Yet ye say, Wherefore? Because the Lord hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy youth, against whom thou hast dealt treacherously: yet is she thy companion, and the wife of thy covenant
debates: Whether the difficult verse asks a question or makes a statement
What the covering of the garment means
Why the people conclude that God delights in evildoers
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch turns the question into a denial that any man of sense ever did this
Ellicott warns against wearing the name Mizpah on a ring
Clarke says they kept their wives till their youth was past and then replaced them
themes: An altar wet with the tears of wives
One woman brought to one man
A garment covered with the violence it hides
Prosperity read as a verdict
